speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deem it a great privilege and pleasure at this time to address the house. As I am making my maiden speech I feel that hon. members might well extend some slight indulgence if I transgress in any minor details. At the outset may I be permitted to congratulate both the mover (Mr. Cormier) and the seconder (Mr. Porteous) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Conditions in western Canada have been outlined by many previous speakers and it would seem unnecessary at this time for me to add to their observations. I would however like to endorse the views of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) to the effect that we should consider such steps as would bring relief not only to western Canada but to the whole Dominion. Many splendid recommendations have been made which if acted upon would bring assistance to western Canada.
First, I want to deal with the subject of our trade relations with soviet Russia. Some criticism has been levelled at the government because of its action in placing an embargo on certain imports from Russia. At this time I wish to compliment both the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the cabinet in that connection. Probably one of the best things that ever happened to the western 
farmer was when the government put on that embargo. I was asked by many people in my constituency, some of them my strongest political opponents, "What is your government going to do now with that $10,000,000 proposition from Russia?" They added, "We will know now whether the Prime Minister and his cabinet are sincere in their sympathy for us farmers. If they are more concerned with the manufacturer, of course they will accept the proposition." May I say that some of my political opponents came to me after the Prime Minister rejected Russia's offer and said, "We are convinced now that both the Prime Minister and his cabinet are thinking of the farmers rather than of the manufacturers; we believe they must be thinking about us farmers in western Canada."
Let me refer now to something that happened in 1929. In that year a trade deputation, not from Russia but from Great Britain, came to Ottawa. Our friends opposite were then in power, and if my memory serves me correctly the Right Hon. J. H. Thomas headed the British party. He proposed to the government of the day that the British government would take the greater portion of our wheat at $1.47 a bushel if the Canadian government would undertake in return to buy a certain tonnage of British coal. I assure the hon. members that as a farmer in western Canada I was very anxious about the outcome of that offer. I expected the government of that day would be considering the welfare of us farmers in western Canada; but to my disappointment the then leader of the government, now the right hon.. leader of the opposition. (Mr. Mackenzie King), implied by the course he then took that "your wheat of course will find its way into the various markets of the world." Had the government at that time accepted Mr. Thomas' suggestion it would have meant to me on my own crop over $4,000.
When I hear our friends on the other side express their belief in the British preference* and their deep concern for the poor farmers of western Canada, I cannot help wondering whether they are sincere. I say this advisedly, because at the time Mr. Thomas' offer was rejected Russian coal was being permitted entry into eastern Canada. I may be asked how that affected the farmers in western Canada. Well, the president of our wheat pool went over to Great Britain and he found a decided change in the British attitude towards our wheat, due to the fact that our government of that day had antagonized the people of Great Britain by turning down Mr. Thomas' offer of British coal in exchange for our wheat and allowing.

7'he Address-Mr. Loiicks
Russia to dump coal into eastern Canada. Again I desire to express my commendation of the action of the present government in declining to accept the recent Russian proposal. In effect they said to Russia, "We are more concerned at this time in looking after the interest of the farmers of western Canada". The best market we have for our wheat is Great Britain, and I am glad to think that today the government of this country is looking after our interests along those lines. Had the mistake of the late government been repeated, Great Britain would have been still further antagonized.
The hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. La-Vergne), addressing the house yesterday, stated that there were more important things to be considered than bread. I agree with him.
I think at this time we would be well advised to pay a little more attention to the bolshevistic propaganda that is being carried on throughout the Dominion. I am a little surprised when I hear my hon. friends representing labour pleading for the soviet government. A few days before leaving the west for Ottawa I was told that soviet schools or classes are being conducted in 121 of our towns and cities. In those classes our boys and girls are being taught to pay no attention to the future; materialism is stressed, the spiritual is ridiculed. In all sincerity I ask hon. members, what can we expect of the next generation if our boys and girls are taught such pernicious doctrines? Not long ago I had occasion to address a meeting in my constituency. The hall was crowded and I concluded my address in these words: "'Ladies and gentlemen, if materialism is all important, then you can endorse the government of soviet Russia or communism; but I think you are not thinking only of the material." Even some of those who opposed me in the last election shook me by the hand and congratulated me. They said: "You are right, Mr. Loucks, after all there is more than the material. After hearing what is going on in western Canada we are beginning to think more about the soviet menace than we did in the past."
In discussing the speech from the throne my hon. friend from South Vancouver (Mr. Maclnnis) said he could see no results at all favourable to the farmers so far as orderly marketing was concerned. I wish to assure him and other hon. members that the farmers of western Canada have been helped very substantially by the action taken by the government to ensure orderly marketing. I am convinced by his remarks that he has little conception of what orderly marketing means to the west. But for the steps taken by the government, the farmers of western Canada would
have been much worse off to-day. If the government had not persuaded the banks to guarantee the wheat pool we would have had to dump our wheat on the market. If ever there was a time when orderly marketing was essential it is to-day, especially when we have such overproduction. Let me point out some of the results from orderly marketing. The wheat pool never would have come into being had it not been for the fact that some of us farmers were convinced that we had to change our attitude with respect to the marketing of our grain. The operations of the old wheat board demonstrated that there was much to be gained by orderly marketing. I hear much criticism of the wheat pool, but notwithstanding all its mistakes I have no hesitation in stating that the farmers of western Canada will never go back to the old system of marketing their grain through the grain exchange. That system never eliminated market depression in the fall of the year. We farmers in western Canada have our obligations to meet at that season. What happens? Every creditor is after us for money. There is only one thing to do, hurry our wheat off to the market. That depresses the market. We found under the old system that individually we could not do anything to eliminate that depression, but that collectively we could. Now our creditors have to stand back and wait until we have received our initial payment; then we pay off part of our indebtedness and later the balance.
I have sat here and listened very patiently to all that has been said during this debate about the tariff. One would think from the arguments submitted by hon. members opposite, especially by those from the west, that western farmers are going to be put out of business by the tariff. I am safe in saying that in my constituency we export more wheat than any other district in western Canada, I ran against the most rabid free-trader in the whole dominion, Mr. John Evans, who represented the riding for nine years. I am told that free trade was about all he spoke of here in this house; I know that is all he talked about during the campaign, but he nearly lost his deposit. I went out and preached tariff, right from the commencement, and the farmers of my constituency supported me because I had the assurance from the Prime Minister that there were to be no exploitations. I have heard a great deal from the other side with regard to exploitations, but I ask any hon. member to prove to me that there has been exploitation in any one case since this government came into power,
The Address-Mr. Loucks

Just a few days before I left I attended a meeting, where I said, "I am here seeking information; before I go to Ottawa I want to know if you can teill me one commodity in which there has been exploitation since the tariff was increased last September," and not a man in that large audience could give me one instance.
I want to say something else, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the tariff on corn. I can see where that will bring about results. We have been told by the opposition that as yet the farmers have received no protection. I feel that this is not quite true; we have obtained protection, in connection with butter at least, since this government came into office. If tariff means anything, Mr. Speaker, it means protection to the farmers. We have received that protection with regard to dairy products, but we want to go further than that. I have pledged myself to support this tariff on corn; before I left home my supporters asked me if I would do my best to have that tariff imposed, and so I came here supporting that proposal.
I think it is only fair that hon. members should ask me a question or two in this regard. The first question I think should be asked is this: "Will you, as western farmers, exploit the eastern farmers if we do put up the tariff against corn?" A question of that kind would be only fair, and my answer would be that we would not do so. Some hon. members may ask, "How can you be sure?" My answer is this:	We know there will be
no exploitation. We know what happened last fall in connection with the tariff on glass. The government made an example in that case, and I am safe in saying that the same thing would rightly happen to us if we should exploit the farmers of eastern Canada in connection with corn.
There is another question which I think you should ask, and it is this: "Are you western farmers sure you can meet the demand?" I think the statistics which were given to-night should leave no doubt as to that. Surely with millions of bushels of grain in the bins of the west there should be no need to worry about that, so my answer is, yes, we will meet the demand as far as eastern Canada is concerned.
Then I want to come back to the subject brought up by my hon. friend who is interested in the ranchers. I can see an opportunity for great benefit to the farmers of eastern Canada who are feeding cattle as well as to the farmers of the west; I think you can help us out and we can help you out. Some of you eastern farmers can come out to the

west; we can provide you with feeder steers and also with barley and oats with which to finish them, and I think in that way you can help out the ranchers. I mention this with no other thought than that perhaps because of climatic conditions it would be good business to cooperate along this line. You could give us a fair price for our feeder steers, as I think you would, and we could give you plenty of coarse grains for finishing, also at a reasonable price.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to something else; I am going to advocate what is practically interprovincial preference instead of empire preference, and I think this question should be considered at this time. In order to make this proposal a success, however, something will have to be done in connection with freight rates. I think the time has come when it is only fair to bring our domestic freight rates in line with the export rates. For years, as I understand it, the domestic freight rates have been about double export rates. As a farmer I received a great surprise when, during the campaign, I made some investigations along this line. I went to the extreme western part of Alberta and found that from Calgary to British Columbia the domestic rate was just a little more than twice the export rate. Under the present system it would pay us, as farmers, to ship our wheat all the way to England and bring it back _ again in order to sell it in British Columbia. I have every faith in this government; I think they will take action and get the domestic rate down to the export rate, and I will be disappointed if that is not done!
I think we are going to show some of the horn members opposite who have been criticizing us that this government is trying to do something for us in western Canada.
Some reference has been made to our banking system in western Canada. I am not much in sympathy with it, and neither is any other western farmer. I am just an ordinary farmer, and I had no idea that the legal rate of interest was only 7 per cent. Surely the hon. gentlemen who are now in opposition, and who had control of affairs for nine years, must have known that fact, but I did not know it. I am told now that the legal bank interest is 7 per cent, but I have been in western Canada for twenty-six years and I have never been able to borrow money from the banks for less than 8 per cent interest.
If I go to the bank to borrow S100, the banker takes my note and hands me only $92 on which to do my financing. I went to the manager of the bank and said, "Are you not violating the Bank Act in this procedure?" He said he was not, and when I asked him

The Address-Mr. Loucks
why he said that, his reply was, "We do not call it interest at all; we call it discounting your note." In that way they get around the Bank Act. Again I have every confidence in the ability of this government to see that something is done to make the banks stay within the law. I have received many resolutions from different farmer organizations asking that something be done in this regard, and I believe something will be done. I go further; I do not believe the farmers can afford to pay more than 6 per cent interest on loans. We will do a great service to western Canada if we see to it that the interest rate is reduced, and I am here from western Canada pledged to do my part in seeing that cheaper money is provided for the farmers of the west.
To an ordinary farmer parliament is rather a funny place, if I may use those words. For over a week I have listened to this debate;
I have heard ridicule heaped on the government by hon. members opposite, but I have not heard anyone suggest a remedy. It seems to me that the opposition have taken the attitude of saying, We can wash our hands of the matter now; the whole responsibility is on the government. If the leader of the opposition were in his place I think I could tell him without fear of contradiction that he would do better in the west, at the next election if he just sat back and folded his arms and did not interfere with the program of the government. Some of my neighbours were at the station to see me off and they said, "Well, Bill, you are going to have a long drawn out session down there, I suppose?" My answer was, "No, I do not expect it; I think there will be a sort of coalition government down there this time. I think the opposition has enough vision to cooperate with the government in order to see if something cannot be done to relieve present conditions." All these conditions 'have not arisen during the last eight months; do not let us fool ourselves. When hon. gentlemen opposite get up here and ridicule the present government, misrepresenting things, and saying that the responsibility for prevailing conditions rests with a government that has been in power eight months, those hon. gentlemen must think that our intelligence in western Canada is not very high. Are those hon. gentlemen going to support us and see that the farmers of the west get the protection they need? Are they going to vote against a policy which is intended to benefit the west? Every gentleman across the way should be nodding his head now in assent. If they are sincere I do not see how they could help agreeing to give the farmers some protection.
But I do not see any of them nodding their heads. There must be something wrong with their necks. I would give them a prescription; they had better get a little lubricating oil, if their necks are so stiff that they cannot nod in agreement with a policy which is intended to further the interests of western Canada.
What is the attitude of those hon. gentlemen in regard to freight rates? They were in power for nine years but did nothing to help us out in that regard. Will they accept the invitation now to lend us their support in regard to an export rate which will help to improve conditions both in eastern Canada and in the west? They should be bowing their heads to show that they endorse what I am saying. If they do not endorse that position they will not be back after the next election.
There are many things I should like to mention, but naturally as a new member I am somewhat embarrassed. Imagine an old farmer living away back in the prairies, and the farmers of the district coming after him and saying, "We want to put this matter into your hands; we know that we can trust you; you know the situation in this constituency and we want you to represent us." I know they thought that way or I should not be here. But let me suggest some of the reasons why I am here. One of them is the fact that we have in Canada to-day a prime minister who was not afraid to go from the Atlantic to the Pacific through all our manufacturing concerns and say, "When I protect you there will be no exploitation." I am glad to say that we have such a man at the head of the government; and so long as the present Prime Minister conducts the affairs of the country in that spirit we need not worry very much about conditions in the west. We are behind him. The trouble with us heretofore has been that we were exploited; but we are not going to be exploited from now on. We feel confident now that exploitation will be a thing of the past.
I received a letter from the former member of the constituency, written in very sympathetic terms, before I accepted the nomination. It was written in language to this effect: "Mr. Loucks, I would advise you to have nothing to do with either Liberals or Conservatives. You will be subjected to severe trials. You will be under a whip." I was quite amused. Of course, as a farmer accustomed to using a whip, I pondered what sort of whip this gentleman was referring to, whether it was a cat o' nine tails or what. I am glad to say that so far I have not seen any evidence of any whip of that description.
The Address-Mr. Loueks

But when the leader of the opposition got up to speak I must say I began to quiver. When he referred to the way in which the Prime Minister was running the country I said to myself, " May'be Mr. Evans's word has come true." And the only thing that I could see was this, that if there was a whip it must have been used on the Liberal side during the past administration, when Mr. John Evans was here. It seemed to me that that gentleman must have been thinking in terms of the past administration when he warned me that I might be subject to such punishment.
Before I close I wish to assure the government, as a farmer of the west, that they will have my sincere support so long as they do those things which they have undertaken to carry out. So long as they take such steps as will help to alleviate the distress in the west, I can assure them of my support; and I have no doubt that, before the session is over, those things which I have pointed out to-night as being necessary in the interests of the country will cease to have been matters of theory and will have been put into practice.

I have noticed that three or four of the newer members who have recently spoken have said they have risen with diffidence. To say that I have risen with diffidence would be altogether to underestimate my feelings at the present moment. I must confess that I have not yet overcome the sense of awe I experienced when I first entered this chamber. When I looked upon the faces of men whose names have been household words in Canada for many years, whose speeches I have been reading for many years, men on both sides of the house, men I have come to feel that I knew personally, although I had never met them or spoken to them, I felt it would be almost an impertinence for one like myself, with so little knowledge, with so little ability to express himself, to rise and give utterance to the opinions I hold. Nevertheless I hold certain opinions that are the result of reading, the result of meeting with other men who have become possessed of knowledge in the political world, and I feel it is my duty to give expression to those opinions to-night, because that was one of the purposes for which I was elected in July last.
I should like to say first of all that I frankly and freely admit that the Conservative party in power to-day is not and cannot be held wholly responsible for the unhappy conditions that exist at the present time both in the matter of the lack of market for our farm products and in the matter of unemployment. I must say however that in my opinion, in the 
matter of a market for farm products, the situation was aggravated somewhat by the legislation passed at the short session of parliament; and I firmly believe, in the matter of unemployment, that time will prove that even in that respect the legislation of the last session has been an aggravation rather than otherwise.
During the election campaign our opponents in the west, and in the east too, were blaming the policies of the Liberal party for the unhappy conditions then existing. We did not believe that we were to blame. On the other hand, we were willing to accept the reasoned opinions of those who were fully conversant with world conditions. I have before me an opinion expressed by Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor, vice-president of the Bank of Montreal, as published in the Financial Times of London, England. He said:
Canada, except for the wheat situation which is slowly correcting itself, has been less affected than almost any other country by the economic and industrial crisis through which the world at large is at present passing.
About the same time Mr. J. C. Waugh, President of Brydges and Waugh Limited, financial agents of Winnipeg, said:
I had the pleasure recently of meeting a very prominent English business man. He was on his return from a tour around the world.
I was telling him of our grain situation here. He said, "You know, your situation is not peculiar. Australia's wool market, Mexico's silver market, Brazil's coffee market, Cuba's sugar market, the United States' grain and cotton market, and practically the market of every producing country in the world, is each in just as difficult a position as yours here. In England we have been going through these conditions for nine years, and I should say that Canada seems to be the last place to have been affected.
I am led to the conclusion that even our Conservative opponents in the west were not quite sincere when they said that they held us responsible for those unhappy conditions to which I have referred. I notice to-day they are inclined to blame world conditions for this situation. I notice that even the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) at Calgary on January 3rd is reported by a Canadian Press-despatch as having made a statement to this effect. He himself did not use the following, words; they are the words of the correspondent. I quote:
Application of temporary measures to correct present economic conditions will not satisfy Premier R. B. Bennett. He is determined to unearth the final causes of the present depression and lay a secure foundation for permanent future prosperity. So he told a large gathering of his fellow-citizens of Calgary assembled Friday at a luncheon arranged jointly by the board of trade, the young men's section of the board' of trade and the ICiwanis club.

The Address-Mr. Butcher
"I cannot make up my mind," lie said, "why this country between the lake and the mountains should experience the depression, why people who have lived here for years should now find themselves without any accumulation of goods, sometimes without the barest necessities of life."	_
Mr. Bennett said he had no fixed idea as to the answer to the questions which came to his mind, but was determined to find it. With a country with the credit of Canada palliatives could easily be supplied, but it was essential to provide for lasting security. The government was confronted not only with a problem of adjustment, but with the necessity of finding and eradicating the ultimate causes of depression.
From that it seems clear that the Prime Minister himself did not believe that Liberal policies were the cause of the depression that existed; but on the other hand he declared that he was setting out to discover what those causes actually were. Notwithstanding the fact that I cannot find it reasonable to blame the Conservative party, the government of to-day for the conditions that exist, I think I am quite justified in again reminding the Prime Minister and his followers that they were pledged to remedy the situation at once, forthwith. The Prime Minister himself said that if he were returned to power he would end unemployment; he would cause unemployment to be a bogey to be laughed at. He further said that he would force a way into the markets of the world for our wheat. Surely we have a right to believe that the Prime Minister was sincere when he uttered those words, and we have a right to say t<5 him: Redeem your promises; you were returned to power upon the understanding that you would fulfil this promise forthwith after your election.
I am going to add that the present Prime Minister did redeem two promises which he made, and he redeemed them very promptly. The first of those promises was that a special session should be called to deal with these matters; the second was that at that special session provision would be made for unemployment relief. Both of those promises were kept. The special session was called as soon as possible after the people had recorded their verdict. At that special session an amount of $20,000,000 was, as we all know, voted for the relief of unemployment; but this vote of $20,000,000, important as it was, for the relief of unemployment, was but a trifling matter when compared to the vote to The vested interests, to the manufacturing interests of this country, by way of increased tariffs. All this was on a special plea of "Canada first." Within the breast of every man in this chamber to-day there is a "Canada first" heart, a heart that beats first
for Canada. I was not born in this land; I was bom in old England. I did not come here until I was thirty years of age, but I will yield to no man in my love for this Canada of ours. I have good reason to love it. It is twenty-seven years ago to-day that I passed for the first time a few miles south of Ottawa. I think the Canadian Pacific at that time ran some thirty or forty miles south of this city; at any rate, we did not enter Ottawa. I know this country has been for me and mine a land not only to have been desired before we came here, but in which we have been glad to find our home during the last twenty-seven years. We yield to no one in our love for Canada, but we say that in the matter of how best we may serve the Canada we love, there is a difference of opinion between us. Our friends to your right, Mr. Speaker, think we best serve Canada by having a very high tariff wall that will close out the manufactured goods of other countries. I had thought of a comparison I was going to use, one that had already been used, a tariff like unto the Chinese wall, suggesting not so much height, as mass, impassability. But I think the illustration that was used by another hon. member was a better one. He used the term "as high as Haman's gallows." May I remind the house of one or two facts in connection with that tall structure that has come to be known as Haman's gallows? The idea of building that gallows was conceived by a great man who might justly have been called the Hon. Mr. Haman.

We know he was honourable because he enjoyed the confidence of his king. He built this structure with three objects in view. The first was undoubtedly to benefit his country; the second was to. elevate himself, and the third was to eliminate his rival. I need hardly remind hon. members that in his design he was at first more or less successful. He succeeded in erecting the structure and at first it seemed as though all were going well. His progress was forward and upward, but when he reached the summit of his career, the pinnacle of success, he experienced a very sudden drop, with a very abrupt termination. The result was an end to all his schemes and a further result was the elevation once more of his rival to a position of power. I do not think it was very kind of the hon. member on the other side of the house to suggest that the high tariff structure of this country bears a resemblance to the structure known as Haman's

Mr. Butcher

ister for making that statement. I assume he came in contact with people who are not aware of existing conditions. I was also very-much surprised to hear the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) say that conditions were bad only in spots and that they might be much worse. Probably his statement is due to the fact that he has been sitting in his well appointed office in the city of Regina and has not come in contact with the actual sufferers. I notice further that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), a farmer from a farming constituency, is reported to have given an interview to a newspaper in Saskatoon wherein he stated that he had had no complaints from his constituents. I would like to tell hon. members that the Minister of Agriculture is respected by all the farmers and townsmen throughout the district in which he lives. He is very popular, but I think he may expect a little criticism when he returns to his constituency. Shortly after the interview which he is reported to hace given I was passing through his constituency and happened to be sitting opposite four farmers who were discussing conditions in the west. I heard one of them say, "Well, we will have to give the Hon. Bob"-I suppose they were referring to the Minister of Agriculture,

"a talking to when he returns to the west." As a matter of fact there is tremendous hardship in western Canada. Some hon. members on the opposite side of the house seem to think that we cannot talk about anything else but those hardships. It may be that we are not conversant with the conditions of the farmers in eastern Canada, but we do know of the suffering of those who live in the west.
I would extend an invitation to any hon. gentleman on the other side of the house who may be disposed to visit the west on the understanding that he adopt one of two methods which I am about to suggest. In the first place we might leave Winnipeg, having met at the Fort Garry hotel. From the hotel we would go to the station and board a pullman car. We would choose our companions, and upon reaching Regina would stay at the Hotel Saskatchewan. At Calgary we would stay at the Pailiser, and in Edmonton at the Macdonald. Having completed our journey we would return to Winnipeg and stay at the magnificent Canadian Pacific hotel. Having taken such a trip we would be justified in saying that there is no hardship in the west. We would meet a few of the wealthy people and our impression would be that there were no
(Mr. Butcher.]
complaints from that part of the country. There is a second way of travelling, however, which might leave a different impression. Instead of travelling by pullman from Winnipeg we might go back to the smoking or second class car and sit with the men who work on the land. We would travel with those men rather than with our wealthy associates, and we would not be long in learning that conditions are much different from what we had originally supposed. We could visit the district in which I live and would find farmers who have laboured from twenty to twenty-five years and are to-day bankrupt. One of the hon. members who spoke a few days ago-I have forgotten the constituency from which he came-stated that the men who went west from his constituency were the lazy ones. I think if that hon. member were to visit the constituency of Last Mountain he would find the contrary to be the fact. In that district there are many men who have worked hard for years and years and have nothing to show for their labours.
I would like to say a few words on behalf of these farmers and with that in mind I refer to the following paragraph in the speech from the throne.
The present situation has emphasized the. necessity of effecting a reduction in the costs of production and marketing of the wheat crop and of providing more stable markets, as the welfare of all parts of Canada is involved in satisfactory returns being received by the grain growers.
I believe there is nothing more true than the last sentence in that paragraph. Undoubtedly the welfare of all parts of Canada depends upon the satisfactory returns received by the grain growers. In that connection I refer to an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on December 16 last. This article refers particularly to the necessity of finding a market for our grain, and is as follows:
And it cannot be too emphatically stated that it is not merely the livelihood of the people directly dependent on the land-there are at least half a million of them-that is in peril. Involved almost equally, though not so directly, are the much larger number of people engaged in every conceivable line of endeavour, who live by serving these people on the farms whose future is now in question: Workmen in eastern factories, railway men, commercial travellers, employees of every kind of distributing agency, dealers in every sort of goods in general demand, professional men, school teachers. Investors-not only those who are direct creditors, but nearly everybody who has money invested subject to market risks-are in danger of suffering heavy losses. We are all in the boat that is labouring in the heavy seas.

Unemployment Relief Tuesday, March 24, 1931
Nothing more true has been said concerning the situation. But hon. members have the right to ask me: "What do you propose?" I have been rather struck by the fact that hon. gentlemen on the other side have complained more than once that we are not making suggestions. Of course not. Why should we? Our friends opposite have said that they know the remedy and are going to apply it; they know exactly what to do and they are going to do it.
I was very much struck by this sentence in the speech from the throne:
The present situation has emphasized the necessity of effecting a reduction in the costs of production and marketing.
What are some of the things that enter into the costs of production? The high cost of implements has already been referred to. Then we have the high cost of heavy machinery such as tractors and separators, high rates of interest, and high freight rates. I may be asked what I would propose should be done. Well, I think it would be wise for the government to do what has already been suggested by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman). I think he gave us a splendid address. He expressed the view that it would be wise for the government to investigate implement prices and see whether they should not be reduced. In my opinion these prices should be reduced. I think also that the prices of tractors, separators and threshing machines should be reduced to something approaching parity with the price of wheat. Freight rates have already been referred to; they too might well be reduced. While there is a flexible shield for the protection of the manufacturer against the winds of adversity, and while large corporations, such as the railways, are assured a certain standard of profit, yet the farmer is not protected at all against the cold east winds. I would suggest that the government advise those who are responsible for the prices of farm implements and heavy machinery, the high rates of interest and high freight rates, that unless those prices and rates are reduced they will not continue to receive the protection which they now enjoy.
But, Mr. Speaker, I feel the hour is approaching when hon. gentlemen want to see the house adjourn, and therefore I will bring my remarks to a close, although there are other matters that I should like to have discussed.
On motion of Mr. Cowan (Long Lake) the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Guthrie the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
